newsitem.title: UK: Halifax to give British banks run for money.
newsitem.headline: Halifax to give British banks run for money.

text.p: Britain's high street banks will be faced with a powerful new competitor from Monday when the Halifax Building Society ditches 144 years of mutuality and joins their ranks.

"The flexibility Halifax's listing provides it with, together with its dominant shares in both the mortgage and liquid savings market, suggest it is likely to be a significant competitive threat," BZW analyst Timothy Sykes said in a recent report.
This echoed an earlier report by Goldman Sachs which said Halifax would "ultimately be one of the winners in the current battle for supremacy in the UK financial services market".

Millions of Britons are set for windfalls averaging more than a thousand pounds as a result of the high- profile flotation. And with the anticipated opening share price way ahead of original expectations, they should receive several hundred pounds more than anticipated.
Financial bookmakers City Index quoted the expected closing price of Halifax shares at 717-727 pence, down from a high of 740-750 pence on Wednesday.
Halifax's brokers Merrill Lynch and Cazenove auctioned 23 percent of its flotation shares on Friday to institutional investors.
Analysts said this will be aggressively bid for by institutions which missed out on the early performance of another building society, the Alliance & Leicester, when it floated last month.
Index tracking funds are also expected to play an important role in the Halifax share price. One estimated that these funds represent 14 percent of the market.

The result of this auction of shares awarded to eligible members who wanted to sell their share allocations immediately will be announced on Monday morning at 0730 GMT, a Halifax spokeswoman told Reuters.
Until now Halifax, like Britain's other building societies, has been owned by its savers and borrowers -- known as its members.
Last February, they voted in favour of a proposal for the society to convert to a public limited company and float on the stock exchange.
Halifax has guaranteed shareholders who sell their stake at auction will receive at least 415 pence per share but analysts predict the shares will be worth considerably more than this.

One, who declined to be named, advised clients to buy the shares up to 720 pence. At this level Halifax would have a market capitalisation of some 18 million pounds ($29.5 million), ranking it among Britain's top-ten quoted companies.
Analysts say Halifax will be a leader in the financial services industry, with a profitable existing franchise and extensive capital reserves -- estimated at more than 3.0 billion pounds.

Goldman Sachs said in its recent research note that Halifax's large customer base, with 20 million existing customer, and strong brand name should facilitate further development of that franchise. But Goldman, which says valuation could range between 522 and 855 pence, believes intense competition in the core mortgage and short-term savings markets may erode profitability in the near term.
It said fundamental value of Halifax shares is nearer 580 pence, still significantly more than the building society's own estimate of between 390 and 450 pence made in January.
